article.headline: Nokia's Long-Shot Call Options and the AI Networking Gamble
article.lede: Poster @seer_xyz shows a screenshot of Nokia (NOK) call options — strikes at $22, $25, and $27 — and asks what excuse investors have not to buy them. At a closing price of $15.29 on May 13, 2026, those contracts require a further 44% to 76% gain in the underlying stock just to break even at expiration, though the same session saw the calls appreciate roughly 33% as Nokia touched a 16-year high.
article.body:
Nokia Corporation (NOK) has nearly doubled in price over the past twelve months, closing at $15.29 on May 13, 2026 — a **16-year high**. The surge reflects a genuine shift in Nokia's business mix: its Network Infrastructure division reported optical sub-segment revenue up 20% year-on-year in Q1 2026, and a newly classified AI and Cloud category grew 49% and booked EUR 1 billion in orders in the quarter alone. That category is still only 8% of group net sales, but at this growth rate it is becoming material. The company also raised full-year guidance for Network Infrastructure sales growth to 12–14%, above the prior 6–8% range.

The strategic anchor is Nokia's 2024 acquisition of *Infinera*, which brought in-house expertise in *photonic integrated circuits* (PICs) and *coherent digital signal processing*. At OFC 2026 in March, Nokia (NOK) unveiled a new generation of *coherent pluggables* — a 1.6-terabit-per-second module aimed at *data-centre interconnect* and a 2.4 Tbps variant for long-haul transport — claiming 70% total-cost-of-ownership savings versus prior-generation equipment. General availability for these products is expected in the second half of 2027; the optical revenue growing now reflects Infinera's existing product lines, not these next-generation modules. Nokia has positioned itself as the leading Western alternative in a market where Huawei is excluded from much of Europe and North America.

The options on the screenshot are deeply *out of the money* (OTM). With Nokia (NOK) near $15.21, the $22 call requires a 45% gain to break even; the $27 call needs 96%. The modest nominal premiums — $2.85 to $3.50 per contract — make these feel inexpensive, but “cheap” here means only that the absolute dollar cost is low, not that the probability of profit is high. The 33% intraday gain in the calls on May 13 illustrates *options leverage*: a 10.5% move in the underlying translated to a roughly 33% move in the call premium because even a small absolute price change is a large fraction of an OTM contract’s value.

Consensus has not caught up with the stock’s move. After Nokia's (NOK) Q1 2026 earnings beat — comparable gross margin rose 320 basis points to 45.5% — analysts raised price targets significantly, with the highest individual target reaching $15. Nokia at $15.29 has already cleared every published analyst target. The average sell-side target sits around $10 USD, implying meaningful downside to consensus before the options’ strikes become relevant. Nokia’s *Mobile Infrastructure* segment — still 55% of group revenue and growing only 3% year-on-year in Q1 — must not be forgotten: the premium multiple (forward price-to-earnings of roughly 30–34 times) depends entirely on the optical and AI narrative scaling substantially.

The underlying thesis — Nokia as a vertically integrated optical-networking champion riding AI-driven datacentre demand, excluding Huawei from Western buildouts — is coherent and the order book provides some supporting evidence. The options, however, are a bet that the stock will add another 44% to 96% after an already extraordinary twelve-month run, within a defined expiry window. That is a wager on sustained momentum rather than a value observation, and the nominal cheapness of the contracts should not be confused with attractive odds.

concepts.definition: A financial contract giving the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to purchase shares at a set strike price before the expiration date. The buyer pays a premium upfront; profit requires the stock to rise above the strike plus the premium paid.

A call option is out of the money when the stock’s current price is below the strike price. It has no intrinsic value, only time value. Deep OTM options are inexpensive in nominal terms but require large moves in the underlying to become profitable.

The stock price at which an options trade neither gains nor loses at expiration. For a call, it equals the strike price plus the premium paid. A $22 call bought for $3.50 breaks even only if the stock reaches $25.50.

Options amplify percentage moves relative to the underlying stock. A moderate gain in the stock can translate to a much larger percentage gain in an OTM call, because the absolute price change represents a large fraction of the small premium. This cuts symmetrically: a stock that goes nowhere renders the option worthless.

A compact optical transceiver module using coherent transmission — encoding data in both the amplitude and phase of light — to achieve very high speeds (1.6 Tbps and above). The pluggable form factor lets it be inserted into routers and switches rather than requiring a dedicated line-system chassis.

A semiconductor chip that combines optical components — lasers, modulators, photodetectors — on a single substrate, analogous to how CMOS integrated circuits combine transistors. PICs allow coherent transceivers to be manufactured at scale and declining cost.

High-speed optical links connecting geographically separated data centres, or distinct clusters within the same campus. AI workloads that distribute training and inference across many GPU clusters drive demand for very high-capacity DCI links.

Custom chips that encode and decode the complex optical signals used in coherent transmission. DSP performance largely determines the achievable data rate, reach, and spectral efficiency of an optical link — making it a key differentiator in high-speed networking hardware.

Nokia’s largest business segment by revenue, providing radio access network (RAN) equipment and software to mobile operators. It is the legacy, lower-growth part of Nokia’s portfolio, distinct from the higher-growth optical and IP networking businesses.

article.fact_check: The “dirt cheap” framing is misleading in a probability sense. While nominal premiums of $2.85–$3.50 are modest, the stock must gain 44–96% above its May 13, 2026 closing price for these contracts to pay off at expiration. The average sell-side price target (~$10 USD) is below the current stock price, meaning consensus analysis implies downside to the stock even before the options’ strikes become relevant. Additionally, the flagship next-generation products announced at OFC 2026 — the 1.6T and 2.4T coherent pluggables — will not reach general availability until the second half of 2027; current optical revenue growth reflects Infinera’s legacy portfolio, not these new products.

ticker_nok.name: Nokia Corporation
ticker_nok.blurb: Nokia is a Finnish telecommunications-equipment maker whose Network Infrastructure division designs optical networking hardware — coherent transceivers, optical line systems, and optical amplifiers — used by carriers and data-centre operators globally. The 2024 acquisition of Infinera, a specialist in coherent digital signal processing and indium phosphide photonic integrated circuits, gave Nokia one of the more vertically integrated optical stacks in the industry.
ticker_nok.recent: In March 2026, Nokia launched a suite of AI-era optical solutions including a 1.6T coherent pluggable for data-centre interconnect and a 2.4T pluggable for subsea and terrestrial transport, alongside four new digital signal processors built on both indium phosphide and silicon photonics. Nokia cited up to 70% total-cost-of-ownership savings versus prior-generation products. New line systems are expected in H2 2026; advanced coherent sampling begins mid-2027. At OFC 2026, Nokia emphasised that the Infinera acquisition provides the vertical integration needed to address the widening gap between AI compute and networking capacity.
